clue.text: Give a hack gin cocktail for confessing to a crime

parts.note: a hack is a dry cough, so to give a hack is to cough

indicators.note: a cocktail is a mixture, so the letters of gin are mixed up

explanation.surface: A bartender's coughing fit, or a mixed drink offered to a suspect to loosen their tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cocktail' mixes GIN into ING. In British slang, to cough is to confess to the police.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang sense: a criminal who coughs owns up, so coughing is admitting guilt.

clue.text: Small firm following price charged for alternative to 28?

definitions.note: 28 across is a cup of tea, so this means another hot drink

parts.note: Co, short for company, is a firm in small form
F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
a fee is a price charged for a service

explanation.surface: A small business charging extra for something other than a cup of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: In a café the usual choice is between tea and the brewed bean drink.

clue.text: Respectable puritan's hot in Utah

indicators.note: in places the puritan and the heat within the state's abbreviation

parts.note: UT is the postal abbreviation for Utah
a prig is a smug, self-righteous puritan
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A strait-laced Mormon who is respectable but sweltering in Utah.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone upright is honest and of good character, hence respectable.

clue.text: Will S's wife come round for some hair dye?

indicators.note: come round means turned about, read in reverse

parts.note: William Shakespeare's wife was Anne Hathaway, Anne H

explanation.surface: Asking Shakespeare's wife over to share some colouring for her hair.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's wife was Anne Hathaway, so 'Will S's wife' is ANNE H, initial and all, and 'come round' turns it back.
explanation.definitionFit: A reddish dye from a shrub's leaves, used on hair and skin.

clue.text: Doesn't care for stormy glens etc

indicators.note: stormy means turbulent, so the letters are tossed about

explanation.surface: Someone who has no love for wild Scottish valleys and the like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'care for' reads as like, but here it means look after.
explanation.definitionFit: To fail to look after someone or something is to leave it untended.

clue.text: Rating little Elizabeth as a superior officer

parts.note: an AB, able-bodied seaman, is a naval rating
Bess is a pet form of the name Elizabeth

explanation.surface: A sailor called Bess promoted to the rank of a senior officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'superior' is the convent sense: the head of a religious house is its superior.
explanation.definitionFit: The head of a nunnery is its mother superior, the officer in charge of the nuns.

clue.text: Inn frequenter and pub Romeo tries to get drunk

parts.note: a bar is a pub
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: getting drunk leaves things in disarray, so the letters are muddled

explanation.surface: A regular at the pub, a Romeo who tries to get drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: The Inns of Court are London's legal societies, so the 'Inn' is not a pub. 'to get drunk' turns TRIES into ISTER.
explanation.definitionFit: English courtroom lawyers must belong to one of the four Inns of Court.

clue.text: A role model, previously rather bulky

parts.note: ex means former, previously
ample means large, generously proportioned

explanation.surface: An inspiring figure who used to be quite overweight.
explanation.definitionFit: A role model is a person to follow, someone who sets a pattern for others.

clue.text: Such a one sends up stars — I might explode with it

indicators.note: an explosion scatters things, so the letters fly apart and land rearranged

explanation.surface: A comedian who mocks celebrities fears they may blow up at the jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sends up' means mocks, not launches, despite the stars.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer or comic who mocks people through parody is one who sends them up.

clue.text: Maybe jousted say for a couple of weeks?

indicators.note: say asks us to take the phrase as spoken, by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: a jousting contest is one where a knight fought, giving the phrase fought knight

explanation.surface: A question about how long a medieval tournament lasted.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a contraction of fourteen nights, a span of fourteen days.

clue.text: Ipswich perhaps draw — Norwich at the top

parts.note: to tow is to draw or pull

indicators.note: at the top of a down entry means the first letter

explanation.surface: A local derby: Ipswich draw, leaving Norwich top of the table.
explanation.walkthrough: Ipswich Town and Norwich City are rival East Anglian football clubs.
explanation.definitionFit: Ipswich is an example of an English urban settlement in Suffolk.

clue.text: Joint firsts in race on athletics speed track

indicators.note: firsts in tells us to take the opening letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: Shared first places in a sprint on a fast running track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' reads as shared, as in joint winners, but it is a cut of meat.
explanation.definitionFit: A joint of meat cooked in the oven is served as a Sunday dinner centrepiece.

clue.text: E.g. write on headstone, a small space, solemnly

parts.note: an en is a printer's space, half the width of an em
grave is the musical direction for a slow, solemn performance

explanation.surface: A stonemason carving an epitaph with careful spacing and due solemnity.
explanation.definitionFit: Lettering on a headstone is cut into the stone, which is an example of incising.

clue.text: Who is missing out on Oscar according to rumour?

indicators.note: missing out on means the first two words lose a letter

parts.note: Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet
per means according to, as in per the rules

explanation.surface: A question about who is said to have been snubbed at the Academy Awards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missing out on' takes the O out of WHO IS, leaving WHIS.
explanation.definitionFit: A rumour passed around in hushed tones is gossip told under the breath.

clue.text: Setter's devious ways

indicators.note: devious means crooked or winding, so the letters are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: A crossword compiler's sly methods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ways' looks like methods, as the surface suggests, but it means roads.
explanation.definitionFit: A way is a road or route, so urban roads are ways.

clue.text: Tired of looking?

parts.note: read literally, being tired from looking describes fatigue of the eyes

explanation.definitionFit: Visual fatigue from too much reading or screen time leaves the eyes aching.

clue.text: The head abandons certain parents — and the rest

indicators.note: the head is the first letter, which leaves the word

parts.note: mothers are some parents, the female ones

explanation.surface: A headteacher walks away from some pushy parents and everybody else.
explanation.definitionFit: The remaining people or things are synonymous with the rest of them.

clue.text: Continental 1D left unfinished

indicators.note: left unfinished means the final letter is cut off

parts.note: 1 down is a hot drink, and an Americano is a kind of it

explanation.surface: A continental breakfast coffee abandoned before it was drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Continental' suggests Europe; here it means of the American continent.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from the American continent; the clue uses the adjective for a continent's people.

clue.text: Sent a late letter last month carried by worker for 7

indicators.note: in a down entry, carried by means sitting on top of the next piece

parts.note: X, spelt ex, comes late in the alphabet
ult, short for ultimo, means last month
7 down is example, so worker for example: the ant is a worker

explanation.surface: A worker mailing a late letter last month for an example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent' is the past participle used as an adjective: carried away with joy.
explanation.definitionFit: To be sent is to be transported with delight, elated and jubilant.

clue.text: He ridicules how ordinary man's entitled to snort dodgy coke

indicators.note: snorting draws something up inside, so the scrambled letters go inside

parts.note: an ordinary man with no rank or title is addressed as Mr

indicators.note: dodgy means suspect or unsound, signalling the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sneering figure jeers at Mr Average's right to sniff some suspect cocaine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entitled' points to a form of address: a man with no other title is Mr. 'dodgy' scrambles the drug and 'to snort' takes it in.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who scoffs or jeers at others is one who makes fun of them.

clue.text: Pick bananas in bed where F1 ones might be found

definitions.text: where F1 ones might be found

indicators.note: in places the shuffled letters inside the bed

parts.note: a cot is a small bed

indicators.note: bananas means crazy, so the letters go wild

explanation.surface: Choosing a crazy fruit in bed while dreaming of racing cars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bananas' looks like the fruit being picked but is slang for crazy, the anagram signal; 'in' then places the result inside the small bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Formula One drivers sit in the small enclosed driving space of their cars.

clue.text: Tabloid paper caught out in debauchery — Public Relations brought in

indicators.note: brought in means another piece is placed inside
out means the letter for caught is dropped

parts.note: excess is overindulgence, debauched living
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A red-top newspaper exposes a PR firm caught up in a scandal of debauchery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' removes C from EXCESS, leaving EXESS, and 'brought in' adds PR. The Daily Express is a British tabloid newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: The Daily Express is a British popular newspaper in tabloid format.

clue.text: A particular type of critter that is kept in glasses

indicators.note: kept in means held inside another word

parts.note: specs is short for spectacles, glasses
ie, id est, means that is

explanation.surface: A kind of creature that spends its life inside spectacles.
explanation.definitionFit: Biologists classify each distinct kind of animal as one taxonomic group of organisms.

clue.text: Unexciting accommodation

definitions.meaning: an apartment, a set of rooms on one floor

explanation.surface: Dreary lodgings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both dull in tone and a set of rooms to live in.

clue.text: Trousers coming from Far East in first place and then Sweden

parts.words: coming from Far East in first place
parts.note: chino is the Spanish word for Chinese, originally applied to the cloth
S is the international vehicle code for Sweden

explanation.surface: Trousers first made in the Far East and then sold in Sweden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in first place' means originally: chino is Spanish for Chinese, where the twill came from.
explanation.definitionFit: Casual trousers made from a cotton twill fabric of that name.

clue.text: A number leaving jazzy clarinet concert

indicators.note: leaving means that letter departs from the pool before rearranging
jazzy suggests wild, lively improvisation, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: N is a standard symbol for a number in algebra

explanation.surface: A performer walking out of a lively clarinet concert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaving' takes N out of CLARINET and 'jazzy' rearranges the remaining CLARIET.
explanation.definitionFit: A solo musical performance or concert is a recital.

clue.text: Standing miserably wet in body of water is a bit simple

indicators.note: standing in a place means being within it, so it joins in to show insertion
in places the jumbled letters within the larger word

parts.note: a loch is a Scottish lake

indicators.note: miserably suggests something wretched and messed up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone standing miserably soaked in a lake is a bit of a simpleton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standing ... in' is one container signal split by the fodder; 'miserably' scrambles 'wet'. 'a bit simple' reads as dim-witted, but it describes basic equipment.
explanation.definitionFit: Technology that is basic rather than advanced is unsophisticated and plain.

clue.text: Setter and solvers drinking punch and Chablis?

indicators.note: drinking means taking something in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: setter and solvers together are we
to hit is to punch

explanation.surface: Crossword setter and solvers sharing a punch bowl and a bottle of Chablis.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark shows Chablis is one example of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Chablis is a dry wine of the pale variety from Burgundy, an example of its colour.

clue.text: Brought over some Frappuccinos and a tea

indicators.note: brought over means turned back the other way, read in reverse
some means only part of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A café order of iced coffees with one hot drink besides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' takes APPUC from FrAPPUCcinos and 'Brought over' turns it round. A cuppa is British slang for a cup of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: British informal word for a cup of the leaf brew, contracted from cup of.

clue.text: Turkey's extra bit of duty extracted in customs

parts.note: TR is the international vehicle code for Turkey

indicators.note: extracted means pulled out, so a letter comes away

parts.note: an addition is something extra

indicators.note: a bit of the word, its opening letter

explanation.surface: Turkey's additional customs duty, partly taken off by border officials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bit of' gives D from 'duty', and 'extracted' takes one D out of ADDITION, leaving ADITION.
explanation.definitionFit: Customs are long-held practices handed down, which together make up inherited practice.

clue.text: Remarking Henry's fallen out of love

indicators.note: fallen out of means the letter has dropped out of the word

parts.note: love is a score of nothing in tennis
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: Commenting that Henry is no longer in love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fallen out of' takes H from NOTHING. 'Henry' is the electrical unit, not a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Noting something is observing or mentioning it, much like commenting.

clue.text: They don't believe article penned by RA as a group right away

indicators.note: penned by means enclosed, held inside another word
away means the letters for right are removed

parts.note: a Royal Academician (RA) is an artist, so RAs as a body are artists
Rt is the abbreviation for right, as in Rt Hon
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: Royal Academy painters collectively dismiss religious believers.
explanation.walkthrough: The RA is the Royal Academy of Arts in London, whose members are painters and sculptors. 'away' drops the abbreviation for right, leaving AISTS, and 'penned by' encloses the article.
explanation.definitionFit: Unbelievers reject belief in any god, so they lack religious faith.
